abstraction.title: Quant 101: Overfitting vs. Genuine Alpha (The 'Needle' Fallacy)
abstraction.core_thesis: A high Sharpe ratio (e.g. 2.4 on ES 1-min) discovered across thousands of parameter permutations is almost always an artifact of data mining (p-hacking) rather than genuine alpha, unless it passes neighborhood perturbation, transaction cost friction, and synthetic market testing.

quantitative_metrics.search_space: 8,580 strategies (entry time, holding period, direction, day of week)

four_rigorous_tests.result: Sharpe dropped from 2.4 to 1.8. Many amateur quants stop here and launch live.

Shift entry by +/- 10 minutes -> Sharpe collapses negative. Change day of week -> Negative. 96% of surrounding neighborhood has zero edge. A true edge is a smooth hill; this strategy is an isolated needle.
Adding realistic 2-tick slippage + exchange commission slashed out-of-sample Sharpe from 1.8 to 1.1.
Permuted market prices with zero edge yielded a top strategy with Sharpe 2.3. The 2.4 Sharpe is statistically indistinguishable from random luck in an 8,500-search space.

abstraction.bonus_warning: Lookahead Bias: The author demonstrated that an accidental leak of the daily closing price at 10:00 AM artificially inflated Sharpe to 4.8 and passed out-of-sample tests. Point-in-time timestamp alignment is mandatory.
abstraction.takeaway_quote: Overfitting isn't a bug in your strategy—it's the number of things you tried. The more you search, the better your best one looks.
abstraction.engine_integration: Implement parameter neighborhood stability sweeps in stock-signal-engine backtester and enforce Monte Carlo synthetic permutation benchmarking before promoting any alpha factor to production.
